_note: Ground truth for roof STRUCTURE, drawn by Josh on renders from src/mark_roofs.py. Every automated signal tried (plane fit, fold fraction, fold depth, fold location, acceptance threshold) failed to separate roofs he calls correct from ones he calls wrong, so this is the only reference that works. Score against it; do not tune against a metric alone.

roofs.structure: TRACED FROM JOSH'S MARKUP (see traced_lines_nztm). Two hipped sections end to end, separated by a FULL-WIDTH middle section that runs eave to eave, about 5.5 x 5.2 m, split by one diagonal into two faces. The 8 faces are: NW hip triangle, SE hip triangle, the NE and SW slopes of the NW section, the NE and SW slopes of the SE section, and the two halves of the middle section.
roofs.marked: red = ridges/hips, green = true roof outline, yellow = the plane surfaces
roofs.key_finding: The face COUNT is not the test and matching it hid a wrong roof for a long time. The middle feature is not a patch inside one slope, it spans the full width of the roof from eave to eave, so it divides BOTH main slopes. The two halves of each slope are therefore separate faces in Josh's drawing, and a same-plane merge that rejoins them is wrong on this roof however coplanar they measure.

traced_lines_nztm._note: Traced from Josh's marked image against the metre grid mark_roofs.py draws (x 1258400/405/410/415, y 5004850/855/860/865). Read off by eye, so coordinates are good to roughly +/-0.3 m; the TOPOLOGY is exact and is what should be scored against. An earlier version of this file claimed the green roof outline was the footprint shifted 1.3 m NE. That was wrong -- an artefact of tracing by eye. Measured over 23 pilot buildings, the best-fit translation of footprint onto roof has a median of 0.50 m in scattered directions and lifts roof-point coverage only 77.8% -> 79.6%, so there is no systematic offset. What this roof actually has is overhang on several sides at once, which no translation fixes.

roofs.middle_section_is: RECESSED (confirmed by Josh). Measured: the ridge sits at 381.42 m, falls to 380.26 m across the middle, and returns to 381.47 m -- a 1.16 m drop. It is therefore findable as a 2-D REGION of points below the roof's own plane envelope, not as shoulders in a 1-D ridge profile, which is what earlier attempts looked for and why their band edges landed in the wrong place.

roofs.structure: Three planes. One large plane on the right taking most of the roof, one large plane top-left, one small plane bottom-left. Josh: 'The largest plane on this roof has a significant angle/slope on it. I haven't marked that. It's also still all one plane though.'
roofs.marked: red = ridges/level changes, green = true roof outline, yellow = the plane surfaces
roofs.key_finding: A plane can carry significant slope and still be ONE plane. Imagery line detection sees a line across that sloped face -- a seam, stain or tonal band -- which is not a roof line. This is what motivated _line_is_real: cut a strong imagery line only where the plane ORIENTATION changes across it, or the two sides sit at different heights. The green roof outline again runs past the LINZ footprint, here mostly on the eastern side.

roofs.structure: Two roof sections side by side, each split by a ridge into an upper and a lower plane -- four large planes -- plus one small plane on the lower-left extension. Josh: '5 in total, with 4 large ones and 1 small one'.
roofs.marked: red = ridges, green = true roof outline, blue = obstructions, yellow = the plane surfaces
roofs.key_finding: First obstruction ground truth. Josh marked ~10, mostly 1-2 m skylights; the pipeline found 4 covering 8.5 m2. Skylights sit near flush so the height path cannot see them, and the colour path scores LOCAL contrast which a bright panel on a variably-lit roof does not always clear. The top decile of roof brightness gives 9 compact blobs -- see detect_bright_objects.

roofs.structure: Josh: 'a very complicated roof'. Two multi-gabled sections, terracotta on one side and grey on the other, with many ridges, hips, valleys and dormers. He marked the lines but not the plane surfaces. This is the exception to his 1-10 planes guidance.
roofs.marked: red = ridges/hips/valleys, green = true roof outline, blue = obstructions (small dots)
roofs.key_finding: Caught brightness-based skylight detection inventing objects. Its threshold was taken PER FACET, and a percentile always finds something -- a tenth of any facet is in its own top decile -- so on this uniformly sunlit terracotta roof it manufactured 8 blobs totalling 21 m2, carving 17% of a 149 m2 roof down to 9 panels against Josh's 7 small dots. Taking the threshold over the whole roof instead: 0 false blobs here, 8 real skylights still found on 29 Edinburgh.

roofs.obstruction_share_marked: roughly a quarter to a third of the roof
roofs.structure: Large commercial roof, 1054 m2 footprint, heavily covered in plant: ducting, walkways, condensers, a large central plant block. Some level changes marked in red.
roofs.marked: red = level changes/ridges, green = true roof outline, blue = obstructions (merged where close together)
roofs.key_finding: Under-detection on plant-covered commercial roofs, and neither obvious lever fixes it. The pipeline carves 16% where Josh marks roughly 25-30%. Lowering HEIGHT_RESIDUAL_THRESHOLD_M makes it WORSE (16% -> 11%), because more flagged points grow clusters that then trip the over-carve caps and are discarded whole -- a mechanism already documented in obstruction_detection.py. Relaxing those caps from 0.35/0.50 to 0.90/0.95 moves it only 16% -> 17%, so the caps are not binding either. The height path simply does not flag the plant: 2021 LiDAR at ~0.42 m spacing against ducting that is obvious in 0.1 m 2026 imagery. This is the case for an imagery-based obstruction detector.

roofs.structure: Josh: "No ridges on robins road, one clear flat face, then a secondary patio roof quite small at the top right. I have marked it as an obstruction as panels wouldn't go there. But the rest of the roof is one flat plane." One plane, 81 m2 footprint.
roofs.marked: green = true roof outline, blue = obstructions (the patio roof and one small object)

traced_obstructions_nztm._note: Traced against the metre grid (x 1258155/160, y 5004940/945/950); good to about +/-0.3 m.

roofs.key_finding: GEOMETRY RIGHT, OBSTRUCTIONS WRONG -- on the simplest roof in the set. The partition returns exactly one face at 90.9% on-plane, matching Josh. The obstruction layer finds NEITHER of the two he marked and invents a third: a 1.2 m2 blob 7.5 m from the patio and 9.7 m from the small object, overlapping neither. The patio is 11.6 m2, 14% of an 81 m2 roof, and 79% of it falls inside the LINZ footprint, so panels are being proposed on a structure that cannot take them. The height path cannot separate it: LiDAR in the patio reads 324.3-325.7 m against a main roof of 325.0-325.7 m, so its top is level with the roof. This is the case for detecting a secondary roof structure from imagery rather than height.

roofs.structure: Three red lines. The two long ones run SW-NE and divide the roof into an upper band, a darker middle band and a lower band -- the pipeline reproduces those three exactly. The third line is short (2.9 m) in the upper-left, beside the notch in the outline.
roofs.marked: green = true roof outline, red = ridges/level changes. No obstructions marked.
roofs.key_finding:
Faces match on the two long lines: our three faces sit exactly in his three bands, at aspects 338.3, 157.8 and 159.9 and fitting 100%, 100% and 99.1%. OPEN QUESTION on his short line: splitting the upper face along it puts 15 points one side and 106 the other, at aspects 337.2 and 338.5, and BOTH sides fit 100% -- as does the undivided face. The LiDAR cannot confirm a plane break there; the region is about 3 m2. Needs Josh to say whether it is a separate plane or the edge of the notch.
SECOND FALSE POSITIVE: he marked no obstructions and the pipeline carves 1.4 m2. With 47 Robins Road that is two invented obstructions on two consecutive simple roofs, both around 1.2-1.4 m2.

_metric_note: Score obstructions by AREA, not object count. Josh combines nearby obstructions when marking, so his object count is not comparable: 'I am combining obstructions together when they are close, so the counting of them might not be the best approach.'
_open_problem: 7 Anderson Heights matches Josh's face COUNT of 8 but not his structure: the central hipped feature he marked is paved over by one face. Diagnosed precisely -- that face is 75 m2 with 11% of its points more than 0.5 m off plane, _best_cut does find a cut, and the setback rule blocks it (cost 2.8 m2 against 2.0 allowed) because one line through a pyramid gains only 1.5%. A hip needs SEVERAL cuts forming a closed shape, and each is individually too small to pay for itself. Loosening the setback rule does not fix it: swept against all four drawn roofs, 2.0 gives 4/4 exact and every higher value gives 3/4 or worse, because the extra cuts are not the hip. This needs compact-feature detection, not line cutting.
